analysis.one_liner: Eliminates interest on all existing and new federal student loans and puts loan repayments into an education fund.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in March 2026 and referred to the education committee, where it has received no further action; it has a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop all interest from accruing on federal student loans, both loans people already have and new ones starting July 1, 2026. Older bank-held federal loans (FFEL and Perkins) would be refinanced into direct government loans at 0% interest, with no origination fee. It would also end the separate subsidized-loan program, raise loan limits tied to inflation, and route all loan payments into a new trust fund that invests in bonds and can pay for loan administration and extra Pell Grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 40 million federal student loan borrowers, who would stop paying interest and owe only what they borrowed. Borrowers with older bank-held federal loans get the biggest change, since their loans would be refinanced to 0% interest with no fee. Low-income students could also benefit if surplus fund money is spent on extra Pell Grants.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Education Department to automatically modify the terms of existing federal Direct Loans so that no interest accrues after July 1, 2026; borrowers may opt out.

Refinances eligible loans not held by the federal government — such as privately held FFEL and Perkins loans — into federal Direct Consolidation Loans with no interest and no origination fee, and preserves the borrower's original repayment term and progress toward income-driven forgiveness.
Sets the interest rate on all new federal loans (including parent PLUS loans) made on or after July 1, 2026 at 0%.
Allows the Education Department to use excess trust fund money for a Supplemental Pell Grant program and for grants to colleges that keep tuition increases to 3% a year or less.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, in the form of interest revenue the government forgoes on its loan portfolio — under current law the federal loan program is expected to generate interest income, and this bill eliminates it. Borrowers who take on more debt also could pay indirectly if schools raise tuition in response to larger loan limits, since the bill raises borrowing caps.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via forgone interest revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill ends the separate subsidized Stafford loan program after June 30, 2026 and shifts students to unsubsidized loans, and raises annual and aggregate loan limits with an inflation adjustment — larger borrowing capacity can give colleges more room to raise tuition, which is the main way loan limits have been criticized in the past.

The new Education Affordability Trust Fund relies on bond investment returns to cover the cost of running a zero-interest loan program; if returns fall short, paying for loan administration and Pell supplements would fall to annual appropriations or additional borrowing, and the bill includes no fallback appropriation.

Eliminating interest on the entire federal loan portfolio forfeits revenue the government currently collects from borrowers, a cost CBO would score in the tens of billions or more depending on the portfolio; that money competes with other federal priorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers the benefit is direct and large: loan balances stop growing, and total repayment drops by whatever interest would have accrued. The main costs are the forgone federal interest revenue and the risk that easier, interest-free borrowing pushes tuition higher, which would partly offset the benefit for future students. The trust fund design — investing loan repayments in a bond portfolio managed by a politically balanced board — is untested and its ability to fully fund the program is uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 24, 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch introduced S. 4169, the Student Loan Interest Elimination Act, on March 24, 2026.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action has been taken since.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat.

The bill would eliminate interest on existing and new federal student loans beginning July 1, 2026, refinance older bank-held federal loans into 0%-interest direct loans, and create an Education Affordability Trust Fund funded by loan repayments.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has changed position; federal loan borrowers continue accruing interest and the federal government continues collecting it while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken and no opposition has organized on the record; the bill's two sponsors are both Democrats, and it has not been taken up by either party in committee.

industries.industry: Federal student loan program (U.S. Treasury and Department of Education)
industries.note: The federal government currently collects interest on the roughly $1.6 trillion federal loan portfolio; the bill converts it to a 0%-interest lender, forfeiting that revenue for the benefit of borrowers. (Portfolio size is general knowledge; the interest elimination is in the bill text [S3].)

industries.industry: Holders of FFEL and Perkins loans (banks and state or nonprofit guaranty agencies)
industries.note: The bill pays these holders off and converts the loans to federal direct loans, ending their ongoing interest income from student debt.

Higher, inflation-indexed loan limits let students borrow more, which can support tuition increases; but supplemental Pell grants and competitive grants are available only to institutions that keep tuition growth to 3% a year or have small endowments.

Refinancing and loan modifications create one-time processing work, but a portfolio that accrues no interest leaves less balance growth to service over time; the fund would also cover loan administration costs.

analysis.trajectory: A bill this early in its life — two sponsors, no committee action, and no scheduled hearing — almost never reaches the Senate floor on its own. Its most realistic path would be having provisions folded into a broader Higher Education Act reauthorization or an appropriations package, which has not been indicated in the record.
